A.explanation: This is the gradient $(12-2)/4 = 2.5$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$, which is the acceleration, not the area for distance.

B.explanation: This value is far too small and does not match any area under the $0$ to $4.0 \text{ s}$ graph.

C.explanation: This is only the triangular part $0.5 \times 4.0 \times 10 = 20 \text{ m}$ and misses the $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ starting velocity rectangle.

D.explanation: The total area from $0$ to $4.0 \text{ s}$ is $(2+12)/2 \times 4.0 = 28 \text{ m}$.

hints: Notice the line starts at velocity $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $0$, not at the origin, and reaches $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $4.0 \text{ s}$.
Remember that for a velocity-time graph the distance travelled is the area under the line between $0$ and $4.0 \text{ s}$.
Split that area into a rectangle of height $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ plus a triangle of height $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ on a base of $4.0 \text{ s}$, then add them.
walkthrough: Read the axes: velocity in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ against time in $\text{s}$. At $t = 0$, $v = 2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and at $t = 4.0 \text{ s}$, $v = 12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Use the rule that distance travelled equals the area under a velocity-time graph, so calculate the area under this straight line from $0$ to $4.0 \text{ s}$.
Treat the shape as a trapezium with parallel sides $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and width $4.0 \text{ s}$: distance $= 0.5 \times (2 + 12) \times 4.0$.
Evaluate: $0.5 \times 14 \times 4.0 = 28$, with units $\text{m s}^{-1} \times \text{s} = \text{m}$. This is option D.
